fields.title: Polka: favorites missing from the schema
fields.summary: In the mockup it is a heart icon, the team named eight weeks. Six until the campaign.
fields.decisionPrompt: What do we do in six weeks?
fields.brief/role: You are the Polka product manager.
fields.brief/company: Polka is a fictional grocery delivery service from local stores.
fields.brief/context: In six weeks, a television marketing campaign starts, for which the favorites section was promised: the user marks items and receives a notification when they drop in price. Yesterday at grooming, the team gave an estimate of eight weeks. You did not expect this: on the mockup, it's a heart icon and one screen.
fields.brief/objective: Deliver what works for the campaign without breaking the core purchase journey before the traffic peak.
fields.brief/constraints: Six weeks until campaign launch. The ad is already shot, reshooting costs 1.2 million rubles and three weeks.
fields.brief/task: Decide what the team does in six weeks and name the price of your decision.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: The team's timeline is usually the cost of structure, not a feature
fields.learnTakeaway/body: When a "heart icon" takes eight weeks, it is almost never about the icon: somewhere in the schema an entity is missing or a relation points the wrong way. Reading the schema and naming the root cause is the product manager's job, not the team's. And then the choice goes down one line: what is missing in data can be filled in manually in time; what is missing in structure gets rebuilt and touches neighbors.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
Entities exist: User, Order, Order Item, Product, Store.

There is no "Favorites" entity.

A product belongs to a store: the exact same loaf of bread in three stores is three separate records.

Price resides in the order item, meaning order history shows the price at the time of purchase.

There is no product price change history: only the current value is stored.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
"Favorites itself takes three days: table, screen, button.

Eight weeks goes to the rest. When marking an item, a person marks it in a specific store. If the store stops carrying this item, favorites becomes empty and looks broken.

To make it work as expected, you need a catalog item uniting identical products from different stores — this is a new entity and a catalog rebuild.

Plus price tracking: you need a price index and a change history, which we don't have now."
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
34% of users order from two or more stores.

61% have repeat purchases of the same item in their history.

500 most popular items cover about 70% of expected favorites marks (estimated from purchase history).

Catalog rebuild affects search and results — the main purchase journey.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
The ad is shot. It shows a favorites screen with items from different stores in a single list.

Reshooting is 1.2 million rubles and three weeks.

The campaign start cannot be shifted: TV slots are bought out.

Peak traffic is expected in the first week of the campaign.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Favorites within store plus manual consolidation of top items
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Five weeks. Mechanics within the store, but the 500 most popular items are manually mapped into catalog items: a single list and exact notifications for them.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
We make it with a week to spare. The ad matches the product for most scenarios: 500 items cover about 70% of marks.
The catalog is not rebuilt, meaning search and results before the peak are untouched — the main purchase journey is safe.
A manual maintenance process for mappings emerges: someone maps new items by hand. This is an operational load forever or until a full solution, and it needs an assigned lifespan.
Some users will get an inconsistent experience: some items are unified, others are not.
Trade-off: you bypassed missing structure with data rather than building it, and this must be said out loud so that in six months no one considers the task closed.
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: Eight weeks. A full-fledged new entity, single list, honest price history.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
We miss the campaign launch by two weeks: the first ads air without the promised section.
On the other hand, this is the right foundation: price comparison between stores, item analytics, recommendations — all of this becomes possible.
34% of multi-store users get what is shown in the ad.
Main risk: catalog rebuild affects search and results, i.e., the main purchase journey, right before the traffic peak. Without a plan to mitigate this risk, the decision is dangerous.
Trade-off: strategically correct and tactically risky; the price is two weeks of the campaign running without the product.
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: Three weeks. Mark a specific store's item, list grouped by stores, item disappears when out of assortment. Price notifications without history.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
We make it with plenty of spare time and no risk.
But the ad shows a single list, and the product gives fragmented ones: 34% of users will see something other than what was promised from the screen.
Notifications work inaccurately: without price history, "cheaper" is determined roughly, there will be false positives.
A month after the campaign, the same conversation about the catalog item returns, only now with dissatisfied users.
Trade-off: safe and cheap, but the contradiction with the already shot ad remains unresolved.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Postpone the feature, launch campaign on the existing product
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: Zero weeks of development. The ad is recreated to match what exists.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
The product risks nothing before the peak, and this is the only option with zero technical risk.
But reshooting costs 1.2 million and three weeks, and there are six until launch: the math works out to the wire and only if everything goes perfectly.
The audience's promise is not made, meaning it is not broken either.
The team gets time to build the catalog item correctly and without rush.
Trade-off: paid with money and internal company reputation to avoid risking the product.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Does not distinguish between lack of structure and lack of data
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Did not see cardinality as a source of cost
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: Did not evaluate schema change as a different order of work
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: Did not account for the cost of index and price history
